sources.title: Dementium II coming to Steam on October 20
sources.text: Atooi will release horror first-person shooter sequel Dementium II for PC via Steam on October 20, the developer announced. Dementium II first launched for DS on May 4, 2010, followed by PC on December 17, 2013. The Steam release is a new, “remastered” version. Here is an overview of the game, via its Steam page : The DS horror sequel, reborn. William Redmoor wakes with fresh staples in his skull, inside an institution for the criminally insane, where the walls keep peeling back to expose something worse. Fight, solve, and survive your way out. The cult classic, remastered. The last thing William Redmoor remembers is the Doctor’s scalpel. Now he wakes at the Bright Dawn Treatment Center with a new wound and an old accusation: the records say he murdered his wife. In his cell, a postcard is waiting. The handwriting is his own. It tells him to run. The staff insist he’s recovering. But since the surgery, reality has started to split, and the “hospital” keeps tearing open into a demented version of itself. The Doctor has a theory about why: whatever was wrong inside your head, we let it out! Escaping Bright Dawn is only the beginning. Outside lies an empty village and a countryside crawling with things that shouldn’t exist. Letters signed by his wife lead him deeper. She says she’s waiting for him. Faithful to the Original. Rebuilt for Today You don’t need to have played the first game to survive this one. Here’s what you need to know. In Dementium: The Ward , William Redmoor woke up in a hospital with no memory, surrounded by creatures that had no business being alive. Newspaper clippings claimed he had murdered his wife. Visions of his daughter led him deeper into the dark, while a man in black who called himself the Doctor watched every step. William fought his way down to the basement to face him. It didn’t end the way he hoped. Dementium II begins where that ending left him: under the Doctor’s knife.

sources.title: Fortnite is coming to Linux so we may soon be able to play it and other games like Apex Legends on Steam Deck and Steam Machine
sources.text: Epic Games is officially working on bringing its battle royale shooter Fortnite to Linux. The announcement was tucked away at the bottom of Epic's widely mocked blog post revealing the new, "vibe-coded" Epic Games Store, which is also coming to Linux. At the time, Epic explained it's going to be working with Linux distro maintainers on a set of security requirements needed to run Fortnite. Distros - short for distributions - are operating system variants of Linux, each with its own goals and prioritised system operations. Valve's SteamOS, for instance, is based on Arch Linux. Because of the many discrepancies between Linux distros, each would need to implement Epic's security requirements individually if they want Fortnite to run on their operating system. Fortnite will arrive on Linux via the EGS launcher, but only if a "critical mass of distro maintainers" is reached. Epic didn't specify numbers. This is big news for several reasons. For one, the move would likely make Fortnite playable on SteamOS PCs and handhelds, including Steam Machine and Steam Deck. Furthermore, even if that "critical mass" is never reached, Epic says its work will be available to other developers interested in bringing their games to Linux. Perhaps the biggest reason this is a big deal, however, has to do with Easy Anti-Cheat, the Epic-owned anti-cheat service used in Fortnite and dozens of other games - including Dead by Daylight , Rocket League , Apex Legends , and even Elden Ring . While Easy Anti-Cheat does support Linux, including for some of the games just mentioned, many developers choose not to enable it , simply because its "Linux implementation couldn't offer the same level of protection as our Windows implementation," as Epic explained in a separate blog post . This is why many games that use Easy Anti-Cheat aren't playable on Steam Machine or Steam Deck . The post even names Valve specifically, saying the team will "continue its open line of communication" to support Steam hardware devices "to the maximum extent technically possible". Part of the reason Linux has been a difficult problem for anti-cheat makers to solve is the platform's open nature, meaning certain - required - system-level protections are not guaranteed. On Windows, you can ask users to enable features like TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot , which create that secure environment once hardware requirements are met. While some of that work can be done on Linux, it requires the interest and participation of distro maintainers. Easy Anti-Cheat plans to use Linux features such as signed kernel, signed kernel modules, and secure boot with attestation to achieve that goal. "These requirements build on work that distribution maintainers already do," explains Epic, "and the more distributions that meet these requirements by default, the fewer players will need to change their setup to play." The goal is to "bring the level of protection much closer to par with Windows". There is no timeline for any of this at present, but Easy Anti-Cheat will test the announced plans in Fortnite first before making them available to other developers. In other words, if Fortnite gets a release date on Linux, you'll know the work has paid off and we're closer than ever to achieving anti-cheat parity between Windows and Linux.

stories.title: I Never Played Ocarina of Time, But 2 Hours With the Remake Proves There’s So Much More to This Masterpiece Than Nostalgia
stories.summary: I never played Ocarina of Time, but 2 hours with the remake proves there’s so much more to this masterpiece than nostalgia.

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: I Never Played Ocarina of Time, But 2 Hours With the Remake Proves There’s So Much More to This Masterpiece Than Nostalgia
sources.text: No matter how much I wish it were the case, I’ll never know what it was like to have seen Jaws in the summer of 1975. Yet, I still get the joy of watching the film that changed blockbuster cinema forever 50 years later, whether that be on towering IMAX screens or wonderfully restored 4K blu-rays. The experience of being there when a film, game, or piece of music entered our culture and witnessing its impact firsthand can never be replicated, but through preservation, remasters, and remakes, new audiences get to uncover these treasures for themselves. This is the case with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. My recent playtime with a demo of the Switch 2 remake felt like digital archaeology; the unearthing of a cultural artefact that informed so much of what came after it, while remaining a gleaming treasure in its own right. A link between one era of video games and another. A sacred text. At least, that’s how it felt to me. You see, I’ve never played the original. Well, that’s a tiny bit of a lie — I did briefly mess around in the opening hour or so of the 3DS port around a decade ago. I know, I should be subject to whatever form of medieval torture you deem appropriate. But the truth is, it’s one that simply passed me by, despite having played several Zeldas since — Tears of the Kingdom is a masterwork of open-world design in my eyes, even if Wind Waker still sits closest to my heart. I never owned a Nintendo 64, and likely got distracted by whatever was happening in my mid-20s, which made me put down Ocarina’s portable version. But now, finally, I’m ready to right my wrongs, and after playing two hours of the remake, I couldn’t be more excited to do so. During my time with the 2026 version of Link’s most defining adventure, I got to play through Kokiri Forest, wander around Castle Town, and complete the Forest Temple. Even from this small sample size, I could see flashes of some of my favourite games within it, and the inspirational sparks it must have fired off into other game developers' minds in 1998. But most importantly, I had a ridiculously fun time with it. From just that short session, I can safely assure you that, if you’re like me and have also somehow let this piece of history slip through your fingers, there’s plenty here for newcomers to enjoy. When it launches in November, there will be little excuse to leave it unplayed. “Anyone who makes 3D games who says they’ve not borrowed something from Mario or Zelda is lying — from the games on Nintendo 64, not necessarily the ones from today,” said Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser to the New York Times . It’s a point that’s hard to argue with, and one I wouldn’t dare contest — I think one of the minds behind GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 probably knows more about game design than I. Nintendo having created something of a lending library for game design is something I could see most clearly in the Forest Temple. I enjoyed unpicking each of its knotted series of corridors and unpacking its hidden secrets, all wrapped in a spooky mansion setting. Every room is a puzzle, whether in the more traditional sense of moving heavy stone cubes around to unblock routes or navigating combat challenges that put your tool belt to the test. Battles are never overly challenging but wonderfully engaging, with looming sword-and-shield-wielding skeletons reacting to your actions as you, in turn, have to counter theirs with a well-timed dodge or stun. When striking them down, you can see the basic structure that would go on to influence Batman Arkham’s brawls — one of the defining melee combat systems — in the way that fights carry the rhythm of enemies reading your movements and you, in turn, having to react with the correct rock-paper-scissors response. Outside of scraps, the structure of the whole temple can’t help but conjure memories of Dark Souls' intertwining, shortcut-unlocking approach to level design. Every route loops back to its central chamber, in which four coloured flames need to be lit in order for the path to the boss to reveal itself. The construction of this area is masterfully done, clearly indicating what you have to achieve without ever holding your hand too much. That freedom of thought has always been prevalent in Zelda, all the way up to how Tears of the Kingdom brings out your most experimental thoughts with its building systems. In Ocarina, breadcrumbs of clues as to how to achieve objectives are given, with tempting buttons placed out of reach behind locked gates and high up ledges seemingly unreachable. That’s until you realise you can rotate the hallways and alter the architecture of the temple completely, like some sort of prototype of Dishonored 2’s Clockwork Mansion. This mechanic is key to navigating the space, and where much of its challenge lies. Entire projects, such as Fez, have gone on to use a system like this to power a whole game. Here, it’s utilised for less than an hour. It’s a testament to the enduring inventiveness of Nintendo that these ideas still echo through gaming today. I found great joy in the simplicity of the temple, but one that tickled my brain enough to never seem like child’s play. There’s a delicate balance when it comes to signposting without holding your hand, to the point where the temple delivered several “aha” moments over the course of my time exploring it. Some came naturally through decades of playing video games, like seeing a frozen target with a raging fire nearby, clearly indicating I needed to fire an arrow through the flames to melt it. But some did give me pause for thought, such as not realising I needed to use my bow to knock each of the temple’s four guardian sprites out of paintings in order to progress. Still, I tried it anyway, and lo and behold, it worked. It’s that sort of “let's see if this works” experimentation that I’ve always appreciated in Zelda, so it’s no surprise to see it pioneered here in the series first foray into 3D. sources.title: The Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Sounds Meaningfully Better Than the Original
sources.text: Previews indicate Nintendo really cares about this one Switchboard is Polygon's weekly newsletter for all things Nintendo, sent on Thursdays and published on the site on Saturdays. You can subscribe here . Guess what — Nintendo's all-in on physical media. This unsurprising fact became news this week after an executive for Nintendo in Latin America made some mild and extremely uncontroversial comments to the effect. "We know how much the fans like it," Bill van Zyll said, while pointing out that the company had just launched a new platform, in Switch 2, that supports physical cartridges. This is only worth noting due to Sony's unpopular decision to end production of physical PlayStation games starting in 2028, but still: good to know. As a family-oriented company which still has strong ties to toy retail, Nintendo enjoys a far higher proportion of physical retail sales than any of its competitors, so this position just makes a boring kind of sense. But it also has more to lose; as pressure on memory chip prices continues, Switch game cards are surely much more expensive to manufacture than Blu-ray discs. Hence the functionally empty game-key cards most third-party publishers have resorted to. But when it comes to its own titles, Nintendo still insists on shipping the full game on the card, and hang the expense. You can tell what matters to Nintendo by what it chooses to spend money on. It typically doesn't go overboard on development budgets for its games, reasoning that expensive graphical fidelity won't add a proportional amount of fun. (It would also take up more of those costly gigabytes). But Nintendo goes out of pocket to put all of, say, next month's Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on a game card, because it is a proportionally better experience. Imagine being nine years old, unwrapping the game for Christmas, putting it in your Switch 2 and then having to wait for it to download. Unacceptable. First hands-on impressions of the Ocarina remake were published this week, and Polygon's Michael McWhertor found it "snappy, streamlined, and polished in ways that make it feel totally fresh." Here again, Nintendo's priorities are instructive. Nintendo has revisited this game several times before, but this time is different. The 3DS' Ocarina of Time 3D was handed to an external team, Grezzo, as was the pretty but laggy 2019 remake of Link's Awakening . But Ocarina 2026, unlike its sister N64-era remake Star Fox , appears to have been allocated to one of Nintendo's precious internal teams, and the difference is apparent. Beyond the lush visuals, previewers all noted how frictionless and responsive the remake is, a huge correction of the biggest historical flaw with one of Nintendo's greatest games. (The original N64 game runs at a sluggish 20 frames per second, and you can really feel it.) Nintendo has the same cynical reasons for leaning on remakes to pad out the release schedule as every other publisher. Games are risky endeavors, and new ideas are hard to come by. But in this case, it seems Nintendo also saw an opportunity to make a classic game meaningfully better, and — just as with its first-party game cards — refused to take half measures. This is about legacy, about brand reputation. And there's little Nintendo cares about more. The PlayStation Portable cult classic Patapon , a rhythm-action game about a line of little marching warriors, has been reimagined by some of its original developers in a roguelike spiritual sequel. It doesn't quite hang together, but it's a powerful nostalgia trip all the same. As the excellent Castlevania: Belmont's Curse arrives on Switch, it's a good moment to revisit this half-forgotten Sega Genesis entry in the series. It's not the Castlevania you know; instead, it's a perfect, technologically impressive expression of a more straight-ahead action game like the NES originals. The strange, funhouse-mirror atmosphere of Ocarina of Time 's direct sequel is captured perfectly by this carnivalesque retread of the "Song of Storms" melody, as if performed by a circus organ-grinder and their monkey. stories.title: Joguei o remake de Zelda: Ocarina of Time e o clássico envelheceu bem
stories.summary: Após 90 minutos de demo, o remake chega ao Switch 2 em 5 de novembro com visual refeito, dublagem em português e ocarina que reconhece a voz. O post Joguei o remake de Zelda: Ocarina of Time e o clássico envelheceu bem apareceu primeiro em Olhar Digital .

sources.title: Joguei o remake de Zelda: Ocarina of Time e o clássico envelheceu bem
sources.text: O remake de The Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time chega ao Nintendo Switch 2 em 5 de novembro de 2026. Ele mantém a estrutura do clássico de 1998, mas muda o jeito de ver e de jogar. Joguei cerca de 90 minutos, e a primeira impressão é de um jogo que não parece velho nem desatualizado. Como estreante em Ocarina of Time, achei o desafio alto. Já joguei Zelda II: The Adventure of Link no NES, mas nunca Ocarina of Time. Por isso, este texto traz o olhar de quem chega sem nostalgia e evita spoilers, mesmo os que não surpreenderiam quem já jogou. As comparações com o original vêm de colegas que conhecem o jogo e testaram a mesma demonstração. O Olhar Digital foi convidado para jogar em primeira mão, e fui ao México viver esta experiência com outros influenciadores e pessoas da imprensa. Jogamos três partes diferentes, escolhidas para mostrar momentos, itens e mecânicas variadas. Primeiro veio o começo na Floresta Kokiri. Depois, uma exploração pelo Campo de Hyrule e pela Cidade do Castelo. Por fim, o Templo da Floresta, onde confesso que travei. Lançado originalmente para o Nintendo 64 em 1998, Ocarina of Time ganhou um primeiro remake no Nintendo 3DS, em 2011. O remake de Zelda: Ocarina of Time é exclusivo do Switch 2 e aparece em um ano simbólico, o dos 40 anos da série. Na loja oficial da Nintendo do Brasil, o jogo custa R$ 329,90 na versão digital e ocupa cerca de 27 GB. Ele pode ser jogado no modo TV, semiportátil ou portátil, e já chega com texto e dublagem em português do Brasil. Quem já jogou outros exclusivos de lançamento da Nintendo, como Mario Kart World, sabe que o Switch 2 tem processamento de sobra. Em Zelda isso não mudou: a qualidade gráfica está linda. Segundo colegas que conhecem o original, os detalhes dos personagens estão fiéis ao jogo de 1998, com um toque a mais de modernidade. Joguei na TV, e as cutscenes são fluidas e encantadoras. O que mais me impressionou foi o conjunto: a arte gráfica, a dublagem em português e a trilha sonora trabalham juntas e transportam você para dentro do jogo. Em uma cena, a Grande Árvore Deko pede à Navi que procure o Link. Dá para sentir o peso da voz de Deko, a pressa da fada e o clima de expectativa. É meio que só assistindo mesmo para sentir, mas foi bem imersivo. Como já saiu um trailer com mais detalhes, dá para ver o cenário e as peças de roupa nítidos, rodando a 60 FPS. A Nintendo não divulgou números oficiais de resolução e taxa de quadros do jogo, e a página da loja no Brasil também não traz esses dados. Na TV, o que vi foi movimento e cenas fluidas. Os comandos de Link são simples: corrida, pulo e mira por giroscópio nas armas de projétil, como o estilingue. Quem conhece o original vai notar o botão de pulo, já que antes Link pulava sozinho nas bordas, e a câmera livre. As duas mudanças foram anunciadas pela Nintendo. O combate tem impacto sonoro e visual forte. Dá para pedir ajuda à Navi em várias situações, na qual ela explica os pontos fracos dos monstros, e colegas que conhecem o original disseram que ela está menos intrusiva do que no jogo de 1998. Esse recurso auxilia para não travar em certos momentos: não se esqueça de usá-lo! Joguei com pro controller, e não com Joy-Con, que, pelo que me disseram, também deve ser tranquilo. Na hora de trazer o review completo, conto como foi a experiência no modo portátil. A primeira parte foi o tutorial na Floresta Kokiri. Link precisa buscar os primeiros itens para encontrar a Grande Árvore Deko e iniciar a aventura, e Mido o impede de passar enquanto ele não tiver espada e escudo. Quem já conhece o jogo vai direto para os desafios. Por causa do tempo, fiquei com receio de explorar demais e perder as outras partes. Não conversei com todo mundo da vila e fui mais objetiva, até porque passei pelo tutorial para aprender os movimentos básicos. Depois da árvore, Link é enviado para sua aventura na floresta. Ali enfrentei as primeiras plantas carnívoras e, no meu caso, levei susto com aranhas gigantes que caem do teto da caverna. Há outros itens iniciais por lá, mas o mais importante foi encontrar o estilingue. Um aviso para quem tem aracnofobia, como eu: nessa fase há muitas aranhas. Não procurei nas opções para mudá-las, mas, como são fantasiosas, consegui me controlar. O Campo de Hyrule foi um momento de exploração, mas, por causa do tempo, fiz pouco. O campo é grande, e eu quis conhecer mais a Cidade do Castelo de Hyrule do que o campo em si. A cidade é linda, com pessoas interagindo, e os detalhes parecem de filme. Entrei em algumas lojinhas, mas me dediquei mais à missão da loja de insetos. A última parte foi o Templo da Floresta. Nessa dungeon há diversas salas, cada uma com um puzzle diferente para resolver, o que leva à parte seguinte. São quatro portas, e eu consegui resolver uma e meia, rs. A primeira é a mais simples. Depois, se você não acertar a ordem de resolução das coisas, isso te trava. Os puzzles são desafiadores e interessantes: envolvem mover blocos de área, acertar lugares estratégicos, coletar chaves pequenas e explorar corredores, como em um calabouço clássico. É por isso que digo que o jogo envelheceu bem e traz de volta o desafio dos jogos antigos. Na minha opinião, o desafio mais encantador é usar a ocarina. Você pode cantar para o console, murmurar ou até usar um instrumento para reproduzir a canção. O microfone do Switch 2 capta o som, identifica a melodia e reconhece a música, e Link a toca no jogo. Segundo a Nintendo, no remake de Zelda: Ocarina of Time funcionam as canções que Link já aprendeu, e os botões continuam disponíveis. O recurso foi demonstrado pelo produtor Eiji Aonuma em um Nintendo Direct. No meu ponto de vista, ele deixa o jogo mais dinâmico. Muita gente tem dificuldade com ritmo no controle, e talvez cantarolar fique mais fácil. Também estão previstas para este ano ocarinas oficiais, incluindo um modelo elétrico da HORI. sources.title: Zelda Ocarina of Time remake has new sidequests, harder minigames, and subtle dungeon tweaks
sources.text: Maybe there are a few surprises to be found after all I can't help but feel Nintendo is being a little too faithful with its upcoming The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake . I know I'm pretty isolated in that opinion, but with new info coming out of recent hands-on previews of the game, I've suddenly got reason to believe that Nintendo is looking out for my tastes, too. The Ocarina of Time remake will feature some new side quests, as demonstrated by longtime Zelda YouTube Zeltik . In Hyrule Castle Town, the guy at the potion shop will now be freaking out about a lurking bug when you first meet him, handing over an empty bottle for Link to catch it. Fulfill his request, and he'll let you keep the bottle and offer to fill it up with a healing red potion. This certainly isn't the kind of multi-stage side quest that you'd expect to have in a modern action-adventure game – and certainly, it doesn't seem that there's a journal or anything where you can track side missions – but it does suggest that Nintendo has designs on offering some things to do that'll be fresh even for those of us who've played through Ocarina of Time a dozen times over. There's also a new, harder version of the target shooting game where you have much less time to hit the targets, suggesting that we can expect some new challenge levels in the minigames, too. Zeltik's video also goes into depth on some minor, but meaningful, tweaks to the layout of the Forest Temple, suggesting that we won't be sleepwalking through the old dungeons, either. I was ten years old when I first played Ocarina of Time on N64, and it set me on a path to loving video games so much that they'd eventually become my job. I should be the perfect audience for the remake, but I've honestly been a little disappointed with how safe Nintendo seemed to be playing it. I know, I know, you can't mess too much with a stone-cold classic, but I already know Ocarina of Time forward and backward, and I'm afraid trundling through a remake offering little more than prettier graphics would ultimately feel a little empty. Offering a few little surprises around the edges, though? That suddenly makes the prospect of revisiting Hyrule a lot more exciting. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's Hyrule feels more alive than ever thanks to clever expansion and a dose of Breath of the Wild vibes. sources.title: The Blood of Dawnwalker Update 1.1 Adds Directional Animal Petting and Over 1,100 Other Improvements and Fixes
sources.text: Rebel Wolves really put out something special with The Blood of Dawnwalker , its vampire RPG where you straddle the line between monster and man. Now it’s getting even better with directional animal petting. Yeah, you heard. Similar to Kingdom Come: Deliverance, Dawnwalker’s combat uses directional inputs to attack and defend from different angles during combat. Update 1.1, due out next week, will let you take that system and use it to frantically rub a dog. “What happens when you merge a directional combat system with the ability to pet dogs and cats?” the studio asked . “Directional. Animal. Petting.” The update also adds a consumable item: the Draught of Mind Rebirth. Take a sip and you’ll be able to respec all your upgrade points and try out a different build without starting the game again. Elsewhere, the game is also getting an even easier mode for those who couldn’t get to grips with directional combat, as well as options for larger font sizes for the subtitles. Accessibility is always good. There are also some visual upgrades coming, such as frame generation improvements, better animations and camera movement, improved lock-on and targeting, and better traversal. The Japanese version of the game has had all the blood and gore put back in, which is kinda vital for a game about a clan of human-sized leeches. Rebel Wolves said there are over 1,100 other improvements in The Blood of Dawnwalker’ update 1.1. That’s a lot, and suggests a certain level of dedication. It shouldn't be a huge surprise though — the former The Witcher developers see the game as a starting point for an epic RPG series. The Dawnwalker team has already teased where that future might take the series one day, with a CGI trailer depicting lead character Coen in the present day . The advantages of being an immortal halfbreed, eh? The Blood of Dawnwalker passed 1 million copies sold in its first two days, which suggests the team will at least get another game out. Whether that takes Coen straight to the present day or flips forward to another historical pinch point like Assassin’s Creed remains to be seen. Kirk McKeand is a Contributor on IGN News. sources.text: A month and a half after the release of The Blood of Dawnwalker , developer Rebel Wolves is cooking up a major selection of improvements to its vampire RPG. Update 1.1 will soon arrive with a long-awaited respec option, alongside animal petting, an easier difficulty mode, and well over a thousand additional upgrades. The respecs certainly seem like the biggest addition. "Free your mind with the Draught of Mind Rebirth," the devs explain in truncated patch notes shared on Reddit . "Forget all your Swordmastery, Witchcraft, and Vampirism abilities, and use the time you spent learning them to master a different set of abilities." In its original form, The Blood of Dawnwalker offered no respec option at all – a pretty harsh limitation in a game where your resources are already tightly constrained thanks to the time mechanic. Unofficial mods quickly appeared to offer respecs, but they were only useful to players on PC. Rebel Wolves is also finally committing to the Can You Pet the Dog? crowd, and they're apparently doing it in style with a whole minigame built on the RPG's combat mechanics. "What happens when you merge a directional combat system with an ability to pet dogs and cats? Directional. Animal. Petting." I don't know exactly how that'll work, but it sounds adorable. The other major new gameplay feature is an additional difficulty mode. The current "story" mode will be renamed "forgiving," and "story" will now get you into an even easier mode with an "additional combat assist." All this launches as part of update 1.1, which is set to land sometime "next week." The rest of the updates come in the form of more general "improvements" to combat, traversal, and the camera, as well as new subtitle and frame-generation options. The patch also includes "over 1,100 other improvements and fixes," so if you're still exploring Vale Sangora, the experience is about to get much smoother. sources.text: "What happens when you merge a directional combat system with an ability to pet dogs and cats?" I've nothing against games that feature simulated animal petting, but it's never been something I've considered buying a game specifically for. Sure, it's nice when your character can stroke a virtual dog or fuss with a clump of polygons shaped like a cat, but it rarely amounts to more than a canned animation. That said, I am suddenly more tempted to shell out on The Blood of Dawnwalker , as Rebel Wolves has announced that the next update to its vampire RPG will introduce "directional animal petting". The Blood of Dawnwalker already features a directional combat system in the vein of Kingdom Come: Deliverance . And this system lies at the heart of the animal petting being added to version 1.1 of the vampire RPG—according to an update the developer posted on X : "What happens when you merge a directional combat system with an ability to pet dogs and cats?" Rebel Wolves asked. "Directional. Animal. Petting." Sadly, Rebel Wolves didn't provide any further detail about this system. But it did offer plenty of insight into what else is coming with update 1.1. Aside from being able to stroke cats at different angles, perhaps the most significant addition is a new Story mode. This will feature an "additional combat assist" for players who aren't interested in mastering the game's swordplay, letting them focus mainly on enjoying the narrative and making decisions. It's worth noting this will not replace the existing Story mode outright. That difficulty setting will still exist, but under the new name of "Forgiving." Elsewhere, The Blood of Dawnwalker will now allow players to rework their abilities through the Draught of Mind Rebirth, which gives you back the points you've allocated into the RPG's various skill trees and lets you spend them elsewhere. That's it for major new features, but smaller changes coming in 1.1 include improved combat targeting, better traversal, in-game camera tweaks, and updates to the RPG's FrameGen tech. In total, Rebel Wolves promise 1100 changes coming to The Blood of Dawnwalker. It's unlikely any of these will relate to the game's controversial time mechanic , even though the studio has said this system might not feature in the sequel . And a sequel to The Blood of Dawnwalker is coming. Rebel Wolves is already working on it after the first game sold 1 million copies in its first three days on sale . stories.summary: Lei brasileira prevê bloqueio de loot boxes para menores, versões sem o recurso ou restrição padrão para usuários no Brasil O post Justiça pede fiscalização de seis jogos com loot boxes no Brasil apareceu primeiro em Olhar Digital .

sources.name: Olhar Digital Games
sources.title: Justiça pede fiscalização de seis jogos com loot boxes no Brasil
sources.text: O Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública (MJSP) pediu à Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados ( ANPD ) que monitore jogos com caixas de recompensa (loot boxes) sem verificação de idade. A solicitação consta na Nota Técnica nº 55/2026, da Secretaria Nacional de Direitos Digitais (Sedigi). O documento avalia os primeiros seis meses do ECA Digital e reúne estudos sobre os possíveis riscos dessas compras para crianças e adolescentes. As recompensas são aleatórias e podem ser adquiridas com dinheiro ou moedas virtuais compradas com dinheiro real. A nota técnica recomenda prioridade na fiscalização de seis jogos nos quais as caixas de recompensa seguiriam disponíveis sem medidas de adequação: O artigo 20 do ECA Digital proíbe loot boxes em jogos direcionados a crianças e adolescentes ou com acesso provável por esse público. O Decreto nº 12.880/2026 prevê três alternativas para as empresas: verificar a idade e bloquear o recurso para menores, oferecer uma versão do jogo sem essas caixas ou restringir a funcionalidade por padrão para usuários brasileiros. Avisos sobre os riscos, divulgação das probabilidades de obter cada recompensa e classificação indicativa para maiores de 18 anos não substituem a verificação de idade, segundo a nota técnica. Pesquisas de diferentes países associam a compra de loot boxes a sinais de jogo problemático, sofrimento psicológico, impulsividade e prejuízos financeiros. Estudos com adolescentes também apontam uma possível relação entre a prática e o envolvimento posterior com apostas online. A Sedigi ressalva, porém, que essas associações não comprovam uma relação direta de causa e efeito com transtornos clínicos. O documento cita a pesquisa TIC Kids Online Brasil 2025, segundo a qual 70% dos usuários brasileiros de 9 a 17 anos jogaram online. Nessa faixa etária, a dificuldade para avaliar probabilidades, controlar impulsos e calcular gastos acumulados pode aumentar a vulnerabilidade a esse tipo de mecanismo. O tema também foi encaminhado ao Departamento de Saúde Mental, Álcool e Outras Drogas, do Ministério da Saúde, para subsidiar eventuais estudos sobre os impactos das loot boxes na saúde mental de crianças e adolescentes. A nota técnica menciona medidas adotadas em países como Bélgica, Alemanha e Japão, além de iniciativas nos Estados Unidos e na União Europeia. No Brasil, a discussão já chegou à Justiça: em junho, a 1ª Vara da Infância e da Juventude do Distrito Federal condenou plataformas e desenvolvedoras por falhas na proteção de crianças nesse tipo de mecanismo. As sentenças somaram R$ 298 milhões. A lista encaminhada à ANPD é preliminar e não exaustiva. A inclusão dos seis jogos não comprova, por si só, que as empresas responsáveis descumpram a legislação. O monitoramento deverá verificar se os mecanismos adotados impedem efetivamente o acesso de menores às caixas de recompensa. sources.title: Governo pede fiscalização de Call of Duty e outros jogos por causa de loot boxes no Brasil
sources.text: O Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública (MJSP) solicitou à Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) que monitore jogos eletrônicos com caixas de recompensa, conhecidas como loot boxes , que ainda não implementaram mecanismos de verificação de idade no Brasil. O pedido faz parte de uma nota técnica publicada em 15 de outubro, que avalia a aplicação das regras do Estatuto Digital da Criança e do Adolescente (ECA Digital) sobre esse tipo de recurso. O documento destaca seis jogos que devem ser priorizados no monitoramento: NBA 2K26, WWE 2K26, Counter-Strike 2, Call of Duty, Genshin Impact e PUBG Mobile. Segundo a análise do governo, os títulos mantêm sistemas de recompensas aleatórias pagas e ainda não adotaram medidas consideradas adequadas para impedir que crianças e adolescentes tenham acesso a essas funcionalidades. Embora o pedido tenha como foco a proteção de menores, o Ministério da Justiça ressalta que o levantamento é preliminar e não comprova, por si só, que as empresas responsáveis estejam descumprindo a legislação. Caberá à ANPD avaliar as informações e decidir sobre eventuais medidas de fiscalização. A iniciativa ocorre seis meses após a entrada em vigor do ECA Digital, que estabeleceu restrições às loot boxes para o público infantojuvenil. A lista de títulos prioritários inclui jogos de diferentes gêneros e plataformas, com sistemas de monetização que permitem comprar recompensas cujo conteúdo é definido aleatoriamente. Confira os games mencionados na Nota Técnica nº 55/2026, do Ministério da Justiça: De acordo com o documento, os títulos citados mantêm caixas de recompensa e possuem classificação indicativa de 18 anos, mas não implementaram mecanismos de verificação de idade para impedir o acesso de menores às funcionalidades. A fiscalização deverá avaliar se as medidas adotadas pelas empresas são suficientes para cumprir as exigências legais. O relatório do Ministério da Justiça também analisou um conjunto mais amplo de games populares no país, mas selecionou os seis títulos acima para uma avaliação mais direcionada. Em caso de descumprimento, as empresas podem ser notificadas e multadas . As loot boxes são caixas, pacotes, baús ou outros recursos que oferecem itens virtuais e vantagens de conteúdo aleatório. Em muitos casos, o jogador paga diretamente ou utiliza uma moeda virtual comprada com dinheiro real para receber uma recompensa cujo conteúdo só é revelado depois da transação. A incerteza é um elemento central desse sistema. Como o jogador não sabe exatamente o que receberá, pode fazer compras repetidas na tentativa de conseguir um personagem, item ou equipamento específico, sem ter garantia de sucesso. Além do Brasil, outros países também já fizeram legislações que proíbem o uso desse tipo de recurso com recompensas pagas. Na Nota Técnica nº 55/2026 , a Secretaria Nacional de Direitos Digitais (Sedigi) analisou pesquisas científicas de diferentes países, incluindo revisões sistemáticas e metanálises. Segundo o levantamento, a literatura associa a compra de caixas de recompensa a comportamentos relacionados ao jogo problemático, sofrimento psicológico, impulsividade e prejuízos financeiros. O documento também aponta estudos com adolescentes que identificaram uma associação entre a compra de loot boxes e o envolvimento posterior com apostas on-line. O governo, porém, ressalta que essas evidências não comprovam, isoladamente, uma relação de causa e efeito com transtornos clínicos. Activision fala sobre lançamento de GTA 6 próximo de Call of Duty MW4: 'Queremos jogadores jogando' A preocupação é que crianças e adolescentes ainda estejam desenvolvendo habilidades cognitivas e emocionais importantes, o que pode dificultar a avaliação de probabilidades, o controle de impulsos e a percepção dos gastos acumulados. A pesquisa TIC Kids Online Brasil 2025, citada na nota, aponta que 70% dos usuários brasileiros de 9 a 17 anos jogaram on-line. O artigo 20 do ECA Digital (Lei nº 15.211/2025) proíbe a oferta de caixas de recompensa em jogos eletrônicos direcionados a crianças e adolescentes ou de acesso provável por esse público. A regulamentação foi detalhada pelo Decreto nº 12.880/2026, que estabelece alternativas para as empresas adequarem seus produtos. Entre as possibilidades previstas estão implementar mecanismos de verificação de idade e bloquear as loot boxes para menores. A lei também indica que é possível oferecer uma versão do jogo sem as recompensas aleatórias ou restringir completamente a funcionalidade, por padrão, para usuários brasileiros. Isso significa que a legislação não determina necessariamente a remoção das loot boxes para todos os jogadores adultos. A exigência central é impedir efetivamente o acesso de crianças e adolescentes a esses mecanismos, conforme as regras aplicáveis. A nota técnica também destaca que avisos sobre os riscos, divulgação das probabilidades de obtenção de itens e classificação indicativa para maiores de 18 anos não substituem as medidas de proteção exigidas. Na avaliação do Ministério da Justiça, é necessário verificar se os mecanismos adotados pelas empresas realmente funcionam. Além de recomendar que os seis jogos sejam priorizados, o Ministério da Justiça encaminhou informações à ANPD para que a agência avalie a inclusão desses títulos entre as prioridades de monitoramento. A análise deve considerar tanto a verificação de idade quanto as demais medidas previstas no Decreto nº 12.880/2026. O documento também foi encaminhado ao Departamento de Saúde Mental, Álcool e Outras Drogas (Desmad), do Ministério da Saúde. A intenção é fornecer subsídios para possíveis estudos sobre os impactos das caixas de recompensa na saúde mental de crianças e adolescentes. sources.title: PlayStation creator backs Sony's call to end discs, says backlash is a "mentality issue"
sources.text: "I don’t think it’s economically reasonable" PlayStation's decision to end disc production for games in 2028 has unsurprisingly led to a massive amount of backlash, largely due to the implications an all-digital future holds for entitlements and actual ownership of a library of games. There have been notable voices in the industry expressing support, or at least trying to explain Sony 's stance amid ongoing component shortages and related hardware price pressures , and you can key PlayStation architect Ken Kutaragi among them. Kutaragi tells VGC at the Game Republic New Horizons event that he understands the pushback to Sony's decision, but ultimately sees it as a necessary step to navigate difficult economic headwinds. "I understand that physical discs have become a metaphor for 'owning' games. I really understand that mentality," he says. "But nobody thinks [physical media] is necessary for a networked device like a smartphone, for example, because people feel that they will keep their content. So it’s a mentality. "I really understand [why some people are upset], but I don’t think it’s economically reasonable. Maybe it’s a mentality issue." There's no doubt Sony and every other hardware manufacturer in business right now is under intense pressure to keep prices as low as possible despite an unprecedented economy squeezed by AI data centers and US tariffs, but many PlayStation users see the availability of physical discs as non-negotiable, leaving Sony and others in a real predicament going into the next console generation. Kutaragi has no direct insights into Sony's plans as he left the company in 2007, but he says he has an idea of the company's thinking in terms of hardware going forward. "I'm not the CEO at PlayStation anymore, but we still have some common [viewpoints]. Right now, Sony Interactive Entertainment has many people who have come from outside, like from Gaikai or streaming companies," says Kutaragi. stories.title: How Should Video Game Ownership Work In An All-Digital Future?
stories.summary: Legislative pressure could force companies to change how digital game licenses work

sources.name: Kotaku
sources.title: How Should Video Game Ownership Work In An All-Digital Future?
sources.text: Consumer Rights Digital Games Kotaku Asks Physical Games Tell Us I love collecting physical games but I realize digital games aren’t all bad. Swapping seamlessly between what’s in my PlayStation 5 library is a lot less of a pain than it would be if I had to get up and swap out discs each time. I also don’t have to worry about my console library creating actual physical clutter in my home, or a digital game getting lost or broken. But I also have zero control over what Sony decides to do with my digital purchases, whether they’re compatible with future hardware, or even whether they’re still playable in a world where PSN servers eventually shut down. So what’s the solution? We’d love to hear your ideas. While my first choice would be for Sony to back off from its decision to end PlayStation discs entirely , it’s also worth thinking about how digital game ownership should be improved in an all-digital gaming ecosystem. Kotaku broke the news on what this could look like earlier this week. Rep. Ritchie Torres announced plans to bring legislation to Congress that would provide the first step toward codifying digital ownership rights. Here’s what he thinks the Federal Trade Commission should guarantee players: Consumers must have the right to own, the right to play, and the right to transfer the games they buy. A game that can be taken away the moment a company pulls the plug is not a purchase. It is a rental disguised as a sale. Families in the Bronx and across the country save up to buy these games, and they deserve better than a license that can vanish at any time. The Power To The Players Act ensures consumers own what they buy and can keep playing long after a company moves on. This is effectively a blueprint for the consumer digital rights Torres would like to see enshrined into law, but there are still a lot of details to iron out, especially for the companies who would need to change how they do business to accommodate the shift, or as Torres likes to call it, a “restoration to the norm” of game ownership for most of the medium’s history. One big question is whether exceptions would be allowed for certain online multiplayer-only releases, or whether those game would all have to accommodate some sort of P2P connection to allow third-parties to continue hosting matches long after the company that shipped the game has moved on . Another would be how to facilitate the trading of digital games. Some have suggested using blockchain technology to maintain a database of unique digital copies that can be resold on private marketplaces. Sony would probably sooner keep giving players the options to buy discs than give up that level of control over its digital ecosystem. But we’ve also seen that things like Xbox’s disc-to-digital initiative can offer people more flexibility with their game purchases. A few things seem pretty obvious though: platforms shouldn’t be allowed to unilaterally destroy, render useless, or lock you out of digital collections you’ve invested hundreds of hours and dollars into building. I should, at the very least, be able to gift my Steam account to my kids, something that’s not currently allowed. Kotaku would love to hear what you think should be done. Tell us your thoughts on digital game ownership and how it should be improved and we’ll potentially feature your response in a roundup to be published next week. sources.title: US Representative Introduces Plan To Preserve Digital Game Ownership
sources.text: "The legislation aims to close the gap between buying a game and owning it" United States Representative Ritchie Torres will introduce the Power To The Players Act . This legislation is being made to support consumers' rights in a way that grants gamers ownership of their digital games. If successful, the Federal Trade Commission could then establish regulations to prevent companies from delisting games, shutting down servers early in a game's life, and easily revoking digital licenses. Some companies are trying to preserve physical media and keep the disc format alive, but physical games are now endangered. With several publishers no longer selling physical versions, Sony ending disc production, and uncertainty around Project Helix's disc drive, the gaming world is headed towards an all-digital future, and gamers aren't happy . Regardless of what the future holds for physical games, digital media currently dominates the gaming market . That is why Rep. Ritchie Torres wants to cement gamers' ownership rights over their digital libraries with the introduction of the Power To The Players bill. At the moment, companies have full control of gamers' digital licenses . Digital storefronts can delist games, cutting off access to a wide audience within seconds. Developers can shut down servers if a game isn't as profitable as they had hoped, stripping gamers of online features promised on launch. As Torres puts it , families use their savings to purchase games, but with a digital license, the software that they paid for can be "pulled out from under them on a company's arbitrary timeline." If passed, the bill would require the Federal Trade Commission to set regulations that grant consumers ownership of a game and protect their ability to keep playing it. Online games would also have to offer a playable offline mode so fans can keep enjoying the game after servers shut down. It is a bill designed to help players enjoy their games for years to come and to "close the gap between buying a game and owning it." Right now, the bill still faces plenty of regulatory hurdles, so there's no guarantee it'll see the light of day. Still, it indicates that the United States government is finally taking notice of issues with digital game ownership.
